sentences.text: It happened at the mouth of the river on one morning in June and it took about four minutes per person and there was nothing to look at.
Xuan had been to eleven of them before he was old enough to do it himself, standing at the back with the other children, being extremely bored.
That is the thing nobody warns you about: the most serious event in the year at Ribadesella is also, if you are seven, the dullest hour you will spend outdoors.
You queue.
That is most of it.

Forty or fifty people queue along the shingle on the north side where the water goes green, in no particular order, and when it is your turn you walk down to where the river is about knee deep and you stand in it.
The queue is the thing outsiders never understand and the thing everybody from Ribadesella would defend to the death.
It is not organised.
There is no list.

People simply arrive between about eight and eleven in the morning and stand about on the shingle, and at some point each of them goes down to the water, and it works out, and it has worked out every year for as long as anybody can establish.
Xuan has watched a man from Oviedo try to introduce a numbered system in 2011 and has watched the entire town be extremely polite to him about it for a whole morning and then not do it.
Then you wait until one comes past.
They are going up.

In the first fortnight of June they come in off the sea in numbers and they hold in the pools at the mouth, waiting for the water, and they move up through the shallows in ones and twos with their backs half out.
You can see them from the bank.
You can see them extremely well from knee deep, which is why the thing is done there.
There are fewer than there were.

Everybody says so and everybody is right, and the counts at the trap above the bridge say so too, and this is a subject that can take over an entire evening in the bar and that Xuan has learned to leave alone.
When he was seven the wait was under a minute.
When he was thirteen it was four or five.

A woman ahead of him in the queue that year stood in the water for the better part of twenty minutes and came out shaking with cold, and the whole shingle went quiet for her, and nobody has ever put a time limit on it and nobody ever will.
When one comes past you say a name.
Out loud, at a normal volume, once.
You do not shout it and you do not whisper it and you do not repeat it, and Xuan's grandmother had told him that people who repeat it are the sort of people who repeat everything.
Then you come out of the water and the next person goes in.
That is the whole ceremony.

There is no priest and there is no register and there is nothing written down anywhere, and the mayor of Ribadesella has for about forty years given a short speech at the start that everybody agrees is unnecessary.
There is no religion in it either, which visitors also get wrong.

The church has never had anything to do with it and has never tried to, and the one priest in living memory who attempted to attach a blessing to the front of it was, by all accounts, handled with the same courtesy as the man from Oviedo with his numbers.
